title: In 64 OpenNeuro event-related studies, the pre-event BOLD level did not detectably change single-trial evoked responses, and an apparent slow drift in response size was mostly an analysis artifact
abstract: The BOLD fMRI level in the 3 s before an event did not detectably change the size of the response to that event in 64 event-related OpenNeuro studies. This agrees with the additive model of ongoing and evoked activity, but the test is not very sensitive, because the pre-event BOLD level is a noisy measure of the underlying state. An apparent slow drift of response size from trial to trial passed its pre-registered test in held-out studies, but most of it came from the analysis. This matters because single studies disagree on whether ongoing and evoked activity add or interact, and because single-trial analyses use pre-event signals and shifted pseudo-event nulls, whose artifacts we measure. Data: ReadyNeuro, one person per study, 80 task labels, 16,623 events; 43 studies for discovery and 21 held-out studies for confirmation with a frozen plan. For each event we estimated the single-trial response (the fitted peak of a canonical hemodynamic response) in task regions chosen without the measured events. The null used pseudo-events: copies of the real event train shifted in time and fitted in the same model. Per standard deviation (SD) of the pre-event predictor, in % of the mean response (59 studies, 95% CI): local level -1.4 (-4.5 to 1.7), global signal -0.6 (-2.9 to 1.6), default-minus-attention balance -0.2 (-1.9 to 1.6), 30-s global-signal amplitude -1.6 (-4.6 to 1.5). A simulation through the same pipeline with a true 10%-per-SD interaction with the underlying pre-event level recovered 33% of it (95% CI 23-42%); the implied underlying interaction is -4% per SD (-21% to +14%) for the local-level term and +7% (-1% to +16%) for the simple slope, so large interactions are excluded but small ones are not. With parcel regions chosen from other runs, the local level gave -5.2% (-9.8 to -0.5), so a small negative interaction is possible. For the drift, the pre-registered excess serial correlation of response sizes was +0.091 (discovery) and +0.084 (confirmation, p = 0.003), but a simulation with constant response sizes gave +0.062 and +0.063. The corrected, time-matched test (real minus simulation, events 6-24 s apart) gave +0.024 (-0.008 to 0.057) in discovery and -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.031) in confirmation; a simulated drift with SD 30% of the response was detectable only in discovery. We withdraw the drift claim; the question is open. Limits: one person per study, a canonical response shape, and BOLD-only state measures.

display.caption: Change of the response magnitude per SD of each pre-event predictor, in % of the mean response; random effects across studies, 95% CI. Grey band: the planned +-10% equivalence bound. Green: the discovery runs simulated with their own noise and response shape and a true 10%-per-SD interaction with the underlying pre-event level; the local-level estimate moves only from -0.7% (no interaction) to -2.7%.

Checks of the apparent slow covariation of single-trial response sizes (activated region): the pre-registered measure, the same measure in a no-drift simulation of the same runs, their difference, the corrected time-matched test, and its drift positive control. Mean and 95% CI over studies.
Mean single-trial response by quintile of the pre-event local baseline (discovery, activated region). Real events and pseudo-events have nearly the same slope; the evoked response adds an offset.
